evals.prompt: We're Trellisway, HR analytics SaaS, about 180 customers, all our data sits in one Snowflake account. Customers keep asking for direct access so they can join our headcount data with their own finance data. Here's what's on the whiteboard: create one view per customer (v_headcount_acme etc.) with WHERE customer_id = 'acme', plus one catch-all view that filters on CURRENT_USER() so we don't have to maintain 180 of them, then put the views and the base fact table into the share so customers can drill down when the view doesn't have enough detail. Our app has done tenant filtering in the API layer for four years and we've never leaked anything. QA would verify it by querying each view from our own account and eyeballing the customer_id column before we flip it on. Poke holes in this before we build it.
evals.expected_output: A review that kills the CURRENT_USER() predicate as NULL across a share, replaces the per-customer views with a single secure view joined to a private entitlement table on the share-aware account identity, keeps base and mapping tables out of the share, rejects the app-layer filter as evidence of safety, and replaces provider-side eyeballing with a consumer-side zero-foreign-rows probe gate.
expectations: States that CURRENT_USER() and CURRENT_ROLE() return NULL inside a secure view once it crosses an account-to-account share, so the catch-all view matches nothing or everything depending on the predicate's shape
Names CURRENT_ACCOUNT() as the share-aware identity function that is safe across a share boundary
Prescribes a single secure view joining a private base table to a private entitlement or mapping table on the caller's account identity, instead of one view per customer
States the base fact table and the entitlement mapping table must never enter the share
Rejects putting the base fact table into the share for drill-down
Rejects the four-year clean record of the application-layer tenant filter as evidence this design is safe, on the grounds that an external SQL handle leaves no application layer to intercept a query
States the engine-level policy must make a query that omits the tenant filter return nothing, rather than relying on every query being written correctly
Rejects verifying isolation by querying the views from the provider's own account
Requires probing isolation from the consumer side, naming Snowflake's SIMULATED_DATA_SHARING_CONSUMER session parameter or a second test account
Sets the isolation gate as zero foreign rows across every shared view and policy, as a binary pass/fail check before GA
Requires the isolation probe to be re-run after every policy or schema change, not only once at launch
Notes the same NULL-identity trap applies to row-access policies, where IS_DATABASE_ROLE_IN_SESSION() is the equivalent primitive

evals.prompt: Paceline Metrics here, logistics visibility SaaS, everything already lands in BigQuery. Two groups are asking for SQL access. Six enterprise accounts (six figures each) want to park a shipment-performance dashboard on it; each one has roughly 50 people opening it every weekday morning, and the tables behind it run about 300 GB per customer. Then about 40 mid-market accounts who'd run a handful of ad-hoc queries a week against maybe 2 GB each. My instinct is that the enterprises are paying the most so they get dedicated infrastructure, and mid-market shares one pooled setup. Does that hold up? What would you actually build?
evals.expected_output: An architecture recommendation that rejects contract value as the gate, ranks the three rungs, keeps the low-frequency mid-market cohort on a zero-copy share, and steps the 50-viewer daily dashboard cohort up to a replicated copy or read endpoint using the scan-frequency tipping heuristic.
expectations: States that scan frequency, not customer size, tier, or contract value, is the variable that gates the architecture
Rejects assigning dedicated infrastructure to the enterprise cohort on the basis of contract value
Presents three architecture rungs: zero-copy warehouse share, replicated copy or dedicated read endpoint, and per-tenant compute isolation
Names zero-copy warehouse sharing as the default rung and justifies it by the data already living in a cloud warehouse
States the zero-copy share is a metadata grant with no data copied, and that live access is paid per query scan plus cross-region egress
Cites the tipping heuristic of roughly 20 scans per day on a roughly 200 GB table, past which live re-scanning costs more per month than a replicated copy costs per year
Labels that tipping heuristic as one practitioner's rule of thumb rather than a benchmark or a measured figure
Places the 50-viewer weekday-morning dashboard cohort past the tipping line and recommends the replicated copy or dedicated read endpoint rung for it
Keeps the roughly 40 low-frequency mid-market accounts on the zero-copy share rung
Names the price of the replicated rung: staleness to the last refresh, plus a second copy of the data and its PII to govern

Names the two conditions that promote per-tenant compute isolation (arbitrary customer-authored SQL at dashboard-or-agent frequency across many tenants, or a shared cluster whose worst-case query already threatens the product) and does not promote it here on contract size
Warns against pointing the replicated copy at the live operational schema

evals.prompt: Bellcurve Health, clinical ops SaaS. Single Postgres 16 primary, no warehouse anywhere in the stack, about 900 customer orgs sharing one database. Enterprise customers want to point their own analysts at us directly, so we want to stand up a read replica they connect to with psql and Metabase. The plan: turn on RLS across the ~40 tenant tables, policy is USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid), and our API sets app.tenant_id from the X-Org-Id header when it opens the connection. We also have four reporting views sitting on top of those tables that we'd expose as-is. Half the team would rather skip all of this and just give each customer its own Postgres schema. Tell me what's wrong here.
evals.expected_output: A teardown naming the FORCE RLS gap, the client-supplied tenant identity, the missing WITH CHECK, the OR-composition and view-bypass traps, the per-row function cost, plus rejection of schema-per-tenant at this scale and of exposing the live operational schema, with the zero-copy rung deleted because there is no warehouse.
expectations: Requires ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, explaining that the table owner otherwise bypasses RLS entirely
Rejects deriving app.tenant_id from the client-supplied X-Org-Id header and requires tenant identity injected server-side from a verified token
Requires WITH CHECK alongside USING on write-path policies, because USING filters only reads and a USING-only policy lets a tenant write rows attributed to another tenant
Warns that multiple permissive policies on a table combine with OR, so a single USING (true) policy silently defeats every stricter policy, and requires auditing all of a table's policies together
Requires WITH (security_invoker = true) on the four reporting views, since a view otherwise runs with its creator's privileges and returns every row regardless of caller
Warns about infinite policy recursion when a helper function called from a policy reads another RLS-protected table, and prescribes SECURITY DEFINER with SET search_path pinned
Recommends wrapping a per-row function call in a subquery so the predicate evaluates once per query rather than once per row
Requires indexing every column a policy predicate references, tenant_id first
States that RLS does not itself grant SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, so matching GRANTs and column grants are still required
Rejects schema-per-tenant at roughly 900 tenants, naming connection pooling and DDL migrations as what breaks down
States that an OLTP-only stack with no warehouse deletes the zero-copy sharing rung entirely rather than demoting it
Rejects exposing the live operational schema to customers and requires a curated mart layer replicated from the system of record

evals.prompt: Quarrystone, e-commerce ops SaaS. We've had a Snowflake share live for seven months with 30 customers on it, built straight on our production tables because that was the fastest way to ship. Two changes land next sprint: renaming cust_ord_dt to order_placed_at because nobody can read the old name, and changing order_total from NUMBER to a string carrying the currency code now that we're going multi-currency. Plan is to announce both in the changelog two weeks ahead, and cut a 'share v2' next quarter for anything bigger than that. One of our customers has also built a certified Tableau connector against us. How should we actually be managing schema change on this surface?
evals.expected_output: A schema-stability contract: additive-only with expand/contract, both proposed changes rejected as in-place, CI enforcement instead of a changelog announcement, a four-part contract, a curated mart layer replacing the production tables, and a warning that the certified connector is a second stability surface.
expectations: States that once customers query the tables the schema is an API: columns are fields, tables are endpoints, and their dashboards are clients
Adopts an additive-only rule: add columns and tables freely, never rename, retype, or drop in place
Rejects both the in-place rename of cust_ord_dt and the in-place retype of order_total
Prescribes expand/contract in order: add the new column, deprecate the old one in the docs, migrate consumers, remove only when nothing depends on it
Rejects a two-week changelog announcement as sufficient governance and requires the contract be enforced in CI rather than by convention
Names a CI enforcement mechanism such as dbt model contracts failing the run on a breaking column change, or the datacontract CLI validating a contract against a PR before merge
Specifies the contract in four parts: schema (columns, types, nullability), quality (completeness thresholds), freshness (refresh SLA), and availability (uptime or latency)

Explains that schema changes are more dangerous than API changes because they often happen accidentally, such as a source-system update or a readability rename, and propagate downstream with no deprecation header
Rejects serving the live production schema and requires a curated mart layer so internal schema churn stops at the replication boundary
Names a shipped additive-only precedent such as Amplitude's event schema, which only ever adds tables and columns as new event types arrive
States the schema gate as zero breaking changes reaching the customer-facing schema past the CI contract check, and that a breaking change that ships is a gate failure even if no customer noticed

Warns that the customer's certified connector package is a second stability surface: a schema change can break its customization file or expected column typing even when the data contract itself is honored

evals.prompt: Northgate Freight Analytics. We turned on Snowflake Secure Data Sharing last month and provisioned reader accounts for the 12 customers who aren't Snowflake shops themselves. Commercially it's a flat $2,000 per month per customer for SQL access. On the safety side we've set a 10-minute statement timeout on the warehouse the reader accounts use, so worst case a bad query dies after ten minutes. Two of those customers have already attached dashboards that refresh every 15 minutes. Finance asked me to confirm our downside is bounded before they sign off on the next 20 accounts. Is it?
evals.expected_output: A clear no: reader-account compute bills to the provider without a cap, the statement timeout bounds one query rather than the month, and the missing controls (resource monitor, queued-statement timeout, concurrency cap) plus the cost gate and the escalation rule are all specified.
expectations: States that reader-account warehouses can consume unlimited credits billed to the provider's own account by default
Requires a resource monitor on every reader account and names it the single most important cost-control step of this surface, not optional hardening
Distinguishes the statement timeout, which bounds one query, from the spend cap or resource monitor, which bounds the month, and states the 10-minute timeout alone does not bound the downside
Adds a queued-statement timeout so queries do not wait indefinitely for a slot
Adds a concurrency cap per tenant or workload so one customer's parallel dashboard refresh cannot occupy shared compute
States that none of these controls are on by default and each must be configured per external warehouse or engine before GA
States the cost gate: every external compute handle has a statement timeout, a concurrency cap, and a spend cap before the first customer connects, audited as a pass/fail checklist per handle
Names the flat-price risk of the unbounded heavy user whose compute cost exceeds the flat price, acceptable only with the caps in place
Prescribes moving a tenant that regularly queues others or trips monitors onto isolated or larger compute
Explicitly rejects raising the shared cap for everyone to accommodate one heavy tenant

Distinguishes capping compute seconds and spend on a long-running engine from counting requests at an API gateway, and requires endpoint-level connection or query-rate limits to stay consistent with the published API rate-limit policy
Names the consumer-pays alternative at the same rung, where compute bills to the customer's own account, citing HubSpot's Snowflake share gated to its top data tier

evals.prompt: Lattice Rail, fleet telemetry. Customer data volumes are wild: smallest account is about 4 GB, largest is 9 TB, and our own warehouse bill is pure consumption, we pay per byte scanned. The roadmap says SQL access ships free to everyone on Business plan and above, because our CRO thinks it's the stickiest retention feature we could add. If we ever decide to charge for it, the plan is to meter on warehouse credits consumed and pass that through with a markup. There's no hard ship date on this one, and leadership has been explicit that they want it to be a durable asset rather than a quick win. Sanity check the commercial model.
evals.expected_output: A pricing recommendation that refuses the free-feature framing, ranks the three shapes out loud, promotes the consumption rung on the two conditions present, and replaces warehouse-credit metering with a business metric the buyer understands.
expectations: Rejects shipping SQL access as a free feature and requires it be packaged as a paid tier or an add-on
States that a price is itself a governance control on a surface that is expensive to over-serve
Presents three pricing shapes: flat add-on or tier gate, consumption or volume-tiered, and provider-pays-compute passthrough
Names the flat add-on or tier gate as the default rung because it needs near-zero billing engineering
Promotes the consumption or volume-tiered rung here and names both triggering conditions present: consumption-based cost exposure of its own, and customer data volumes spanning orders of magnitude
Rejects metering on warehouse credits because a non-technical buyer cannot predict them
Requires metering on a business unit the buyer already understands, citing Stripe Sigma tiering on monthly charge volume with queries themselves unmetered
States the pricing metric is revisable after launch, citing Sigma having changed its own pricing model after shipping
States the ranking explicitly across efficiency, effort, and value rather than leaving it implied by the order the options are listed in
Names the consumption rung as the starved option, highest value and highest effort so it loses every efficiency round, and states the condition that promotes it anyway
Uses the stated compounding-asset mandate and the absence of a ship date to promote the consumption rung, noting that retrofitting a meter under a shipped flat price is a customer-facing repricing

evals.prompt: Vantridge, product analytics SaaS. Everything runs on one shared ClickHouse cluster and our query language is VQL, our own SQL-ish dialect. About 60 customers are asking to point Tableau and Power BI at their event data. Engineering's proposal: write our own Type-4 JDBC driver that speaks VQL, point it straight at the shared cluster, and get it certified with Tableau and Power BI. They've scoped it at a sprint or two and then it's done. Sales wants it live in 6 weeks. What am I signing up for?
evals.expected_output: A connectivity design that names the custom dialect as the anti-pattern, routes to a standard wire protocol over per-tenant engines, and prices the certification tax as ongoing engineering with the specific per-tool requirements, while refusing to admit customer SQL onto the shared cluster.
expectations: Names the custom VQL dialect as the anti-pattern, since a language not already widely supported makes every BI-tool integration start from zero

Recommends speaking an existing wire protocol, specifically a Postgres wire-protocol endpoint, as the cheapest connectivity rung, because every BI tool, psql, and every ORM already ships a Postgres driver
States the cost of the wire-protocol rung: commitment to the Postgres dialect and its type system, and nothing exotic
Rejects the 'a sprint or two and then it's done' scoping and frames BI-tool support as an ongoing certification tax budgeted as continuing engineering rather than a one-time integration
Requires accurate SQLSTATEs if a driver is shipped, specifically SQLSTATE 28000 for invalid credentials, warning that a generic error instead can break Tableau connector behavior
Names signed per-tool connector packages whose signing certificates expire and must be renewed on a schedule
States that Power BI certification requires documented customer demand via a public ideas-forum thread and submission by pull request to Microsoft's connector repository
States that certification transfers distribution but not support, with first-line connectivity issues routed back to the data-source owner
Rejects admitting arbitrary customer SQL onto the shared production ClickHouse cluster, naming the blast radius across the whole application
Recommends single-tenant or per-organization engine instances fronted by one wire-protocol endpoint as the fix for the isolation and connectivity problems at once

Names engine drift as a distinct risk: a query engine changing results between releases or depending on enabled settings, which a vendor's own regression suite never covers across arbitrary customer query shapes

Requires a connection-setup page per supported client covering the URL template, the driver class or download, the auth method, and TLS stated as an explicit requirement rather than left to client defaults

evals.prompt: Orchard Bay, retail ops SaaS. 'Data sharing' is on our quarterly plan and I'm now fairly sure the four people who put it there meant four different things. Sales wants our three biggest partner agencies to see aggregate data across the brands they manage. Engineering wants to stop one customer's monster report from slowing the shared analytics database for everybody else. Twelve customers have asked to point Looker at their own data. And two customers just want a nightly Parquet file dropped into their own S3 bucket. Head of Product wants one project that covers all of it. Where do I even start?
evals.expected_output: A disambiguation that splits the request into distinct problems, names which one is customer-facing SQL access, hands the Parquet request to bulk file delivery, and runs the consumer inventory and architecture-gating questions before recommending anything.
expectations: Separates the request into distinct problems rather than designing a single surface that covers all four asks
Labels the partner-agency request as sharing data with partner organizations, which reuses the sharing mechanics but is not the same problem

Labels the shared-analytics-database contention as isolating compute per tenant inside the product's own analytics, an internal architecture concern, and states the pricing and BI-connectivity work do not apply to it
Labels the Looker request as giving customers a queryable SQL endpoint to their own data, and identifies it as the one needing the full design
States the answer to which problem this is must be written down explicitly, because a design that answers the wrong one ships the wrong isolation primitive
Routes the nightly Parquet drop to bulk file delivery rather than the live SQL surface, drawing the boundary at live queries versus periodic files
Names the sibling bulk data sharing skill as the handoff target for the Parquet request
Inventories the concrete consumers with their expected query shape, such as dashboard refresh, ad-hoc exploration, scheduled extract, and agent traffic
States that a BI-tool consumer needs a certified driver, stable column names, and predictable types, because they never read the docs, only their tool's connection dialog
Asks where the data lives today and asks for scan-frequency evidence with table sizes before recommending any architecture rung
States the design targets the most demanding consumer type present rather than the average one

evals.prompt: Ferncroft Labs, lab-instrument telemetry SaaS running on Databricks. We're standing up Delta Sharing for 40 customers. Isolation plan: set a recipient property per customer and rely on partition filtering on tenant_id, since every table is already partitioned that way, so a recipient physically only reads their own partitions. Credentials: issue each customer a database username and password that they paste into Tableau or Power BI, and we rotate them once a year over email. Our own data team's service account has its password inline in the Airflow connection string, which has been fine internally. Review the isolation and credential design.
evals.expected_output: A review that demotes partition filtering to a performance optimization and moves isolation into a dynamic view predicate on the recipient identity, then rewrites the credential design up the ladder with key-pair JWTs for automation, OAuth with PKCE for BI tools, a stated degradation path, and self-service revocation.
expectations: Rejects recipient-property partition filtering as an access-control mechanism, stating it is documented as a best-effort performance optimization
Requires hard isolation to come from a dynamic view predicate filtered on current_recipient(), not from partition pruning
Gives the credential preference order: short-lived token, then managed secret, then static password
Names the inline credential in the Airflow connection string as the anti-pattern that no documented path should show
Replaces the service-account password with key-pair authentication signing a short-lived JWT, so no password crosses the network
Requires marking machine identities as service-type so the engine refuses password auth for them and the password fallback is closed
Replaces the pasted BI-tool passwords with OAuth, using the authorization-code grant with PKCE for desktop BI tools, so the tool never stores a database password

States the degradation path: a client that cannot hold and refresh a token falls back to key-pair or a PAT service account, never to a static password, and requires verifying each supported client's refresh capability before promising OAuth everywhere
Rejects annual rotation over email as the design and requires customer self-service issuance and revocation in the product
Scopes every credential to one tenant's entitlement mapping by construction and states TLS as an explicit named requirement rather than a client-library default
Notes the industry trajectory retiring static database passwords, citing a staged deprecation that moves service users onto key-pair, OAuth, PAT, or workload identity
